name: Pygeum (Prunus africana bark extract)
short: In rats, a month of extract by mouth caused some toxic effects; kidney, muscle and/or heart suspected (animal study). Short trials in men with prostate enlargement: adverse effects mild, like placebo.
text: A Cochrane systematic review of 18 randomized controlled trials in 1,562 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia (Pygeum alone or in combination, the abstract does not say with what; mean duration 64 days, range 30 to 122) found adverse effects mild and comparable to placebo, with similar dropout rates (13% with Pygeum, 11% with placebo); the reviewers noted the studies were small, short and used varied doses and preparations, and the abstract does not list which adverse effects occurred. An overview of systematic reviews described the adverse effects of Pygeum and other supplements for benign prostatic hyperplasia as mild and infrequent, but noted that the review on Pygeum had not been updated since 2000. Longer human data are limited: in one randomized trial comparing two dosing schedules of Pygeum, without a placebo group, followed by an open 10-month extension (209 men completed the 2-month phase, 174 entered the extension), the safety profile was described as similar between the two schedules and the study phases. In an animal study, male rats given Pygeum extract by mouth for 30 days at two doses showed higher creatinine at both doses (statistically significant only at the higher dose), increased LDH at both doses, and, at the higher dose, a significantly higher liver-to-body-weight ratio than the water-fed control group; the authors said both doses, particularly the higher one, caused some toxic effects, suspected kidney, skeletal muscle and/or heart muscle as target sites of toxicity, and called for further research. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
